question: According to Girls Who Code, how long did it take in years for the percentage of computer scientists that were women to change by 13% from a starting point of 37%?

history.name: user
history.content: According to Girls Who Code, how long did it take in years for the percentage of computer scientists that were women to change by 13% from a starting point of 37%?

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content:
Task: Determine, per Girls Who Code, how many years it took for the share of women among computer scientists to change by 13% from a starting point of 37%.
Plan:
- Identify the time interval linked to the 37% starting point and the 13% change (implied to 24%).
- Prefer authoritative Girls Who Code materials.
- Compute the year difference between the starting and ending points once we identify both years.
Initial thought: We have a local archive of organizational reports and fact sheets. I’ll check those first to save time before cross-validating on the web.

history.content: Acknowledged. The key is to find the endpoint year associated with the 24% figure in Girls Who Code materials. Once we have start and end years, we’ll compute the difference.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: FileSurfer, scan the local documents repository for Girls Who Code reports, fact sheets, or About pages mentioning: “In 1995, 37% of computer scientists were women. Today, it’s 24%.” Extract any associated publication years and context for “today.”

history.content:

- File: /docs/GWC/GWC-Annual-Report-2019.pdf — Infographic reiterates the 37% to 24% contrast; the report is dated 2019.
- File: /docs/GWC/Cracking_the_Gender_Code_Accenture_2016.pdf — Background research; does not explicitly tie the 24% “today” to a specific year, but the report publication date is 2016.
Preliminary inference from local files: The “today = 24%” statement is presented in 2019 materials; absent other context, “today” likely refers to 2019 in these local copies.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Thanks. Let’s quickly cross-check the current Girls Who Code About page to see if the statement persists and whether a year is mentioned.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Opened Girls Who Code About Us page. Visible text includes: “In 1995, 37% of computer scientists were women. Today, it’s only 24%.” There is no explicit year attached to “today” on the page. No clear date stamp appears next to the statistic.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Understood. The live page doesn’t specify the year for “today.” Given our local archive shows the same language on 2019 materials, we can provisionally treat 2019 as the endpoint year tied to 24%. Assistant, compute the interval from 1995 to 2019 and confirm that the 13% change corresponds to 37% -> 24%.

history.name: Assistant
history.content:
Computation:
- If start is 1995 at 37% and endpoint is 2019 at 24%, the change is 37% – 24% = 13 percentage points.
- Years elapsed: 2019 – 1995 = 24 years.
The numbers align: a 13% drop over 24 years (assuming “today” corresponds to 2019).

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Before finalizing, let’s see if any other local documents mention the 24% figure with a different year (e.g., 2018 or 2020) to ensure 2019 is the best-supported endpoint in our materials.

Conclusion: The 24% phrasing appears across 2018–2020 materials in our local archive; the only explicit, date-tied items we have are the 2019 About HTML snapshot and the 2019 Annual Report PDF.

No clear third-party statement pins “today” explicitly to 2019.

history.name: Orchestrator

history.content: Wayback snapshot circa mid-2019 for girlswhocode.com/about-us shows the same sentence: “In 1995, 37% of computer scientists were women. Today, it’s only 24%.” No explicit date is tied to the word “today,” but the snapshot confirms the phrasing existed in 2019.

mistake_reason: At step 3, Orchestrator inappropriately selected FileSurfer (a local file tool) to retrieve a public Girls Who Code statistic that should have been sourced from authoritative web materials or handled by internal knowledge/arithmetic. This tool selection error (FM-4.3) anchored the team on an outdated local 2019 document where “today” was implicitly 2019, leading them to compute 1995→2019 = 24 years instead of identifying the correct endpoint (2017) and the correct duration of 22 years.
